g8-2023-026.activity: Is It Filling Up or Draining Out?
g8-2023-026.quote: Which tank started out with more water?
g8-2023-026.why: The item gives Function A as a verbal description ($3.00 base plus $2.00 per mile) and Function B as the equation y = 3x + 2, and asks which has the greater rate of change and which the greater initial value. This activity is built on that exact pairing: Tank A arrives as A = 200 + 8t and Tank B as a description that starts at 400 gallons and drops 5 gallons per minute, and students compare starting amounts and rates across the two forms. The losing reading, 8.5.7 Connecting Representations of Functions, is second best because its activities do compare functions in different representations but always about particular input-output values (a temperature at a time, a volume at r = 3) -- no activity in Lesson 7 asks for a rate of change or an initial value at all.

g8-2023-045.quote: What is the value of the rate of change for each situation
g8-2023-045.why: The item sets a table (pairs -5/-30, -3/-18, 2/12, 4/24, so a rate of 6) against a graphed line rising 3 over 6, and asks which function has the greater rate of change and what each rate is. This required activity asks that question twice over, once with Elena's equation y = 8.40x against Jada's $7 per hour description and once with Han's description against Clare's table, each time naming the value of the rate of change and comparing. The losing reading, 8.5.9 Linear Models, is second best because Lesson 9 is about whether data can be modelled by a line at all (the candle, the moon, the recycling graph), never about computing and comparing two rates; the only Unit 5 activity that compares rates across representations, Lesson 8's 'Which Is Growing Faster?', is optional, so the required Unit 3 activity wins.

g8-2023-048.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
g8-2023-048.quote: there is one graph that is not linear and match that graph with the equation
g8-2023-048.why: The item gives three functions -- the equation y = 2x + 3, a table of the squaring pairs, and a straight line through the origin -- and asks for each whether it is linear or nonlinear, with the properties named. This activity is the one place in the grade-8 course where an equation is sorted as not linear: students match d = 60t, q = 50 - 0.4d and A = pi r^2 to their graphs and are monitored for recognising which graph and which equation is not linear. The losing reading, 8.5.7 Connecting Representations of Functions, is second best because it has the item's surface shape -- three representations side by side -- but no Lesson 7 activity ever asks whether a function is linear; that is topical similarity rather than the item's question. The table half of the item is closer to Lesson 9's Candlelight warm-up, where linearity is judged from numeric pairs.

g8-2024-001.activity: Is It Filling Up or Draining Out?
g8-2024-001.quote: Write an equation representing the relationship between B and t
g8-2024-001.why: The item gives a story with a per-unit rate ($15.00 a ticket) and one flat charge ($8.99 of popcorn) and asks which equation gives the total, c = 15n + 8.99. In this activity Tank B is described the same way -- a starting amount of 400 gallons and a steady 5 gallons per minute -- and students are told to write its equation, which is the mx + b translation the item wants. The losing reading, 8.5.3 Equations for Functions, is second best because its matching activity does ask students to write an equation for a description, but its descriptions are single-rule (C = 2 pi r, d = 60t, v = s^3) with only the decontextualized 'triple the input and subtract 4' carrying a constant term; Lesson 8 is where a rate and a one-time amount appear together in a context.

g8-2024-007.activity: Is It Filling Up or Draining Out?
g8-2024-007.quote: connect initial value and slope, which they learned about in a previous unit
g8-2024-007.why: Electrician A comes as the equation C = 25x + 50 and Electrician B as a table (130 at 3 h, 150 at 4, 170 at 5), and the item asks which has the greater initial fee and which the greater hourly rate. This activity is the curriculum's place for reading initial value and rate of change out of differently represented linear functions and comparing them. The losing reading, 8.5.7 Connecting Representations of Functions, is second best for the same reason as the other 8.F.2 items: it compares representations but never on rate and initial value. Medium confidence because the activity pairs an equation with a prose description, not with a table -- no Unit 5 activity compares an equation to a table -- so the table-to-rate step is borrowed from Unit 3.

g8-2024-010.quote: Cone with a height of 8 centimeters and a radius of 3 centimeters.
g8-2024-010.why: The item asks for an expression, not a number: the volume of a sphere of radius 4 minus the volume of a cone of radius 3 and height 8, with distractors that swap r^3 for r^2 in the sphere formula and swap the cone's radius and height. This activity is the one place students apply the sphere and cone formulas to figures with independently given dimensions and compare the results, and its cone is literally radius 3, height 8. The losing reading, 8.5.20 The Volume of a Sphere, is second best because Lesson 20 derives 4/3 pi r^3 and its cool-down does ask for a sphere of radius 4 in terms of pi, but its cone and sphere always share a radius and height, so it never asks the item's two-formulas-two-sets-of-dimensions question. Flagged optional: the non-optional runner-up is Lesson 21's warm-up 'Sphere Arguments' (page 292), which targets exactly the item's sphere-formula distractors -- using r instead of r^3 and dropping pi.

g8-2024-020.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
g8-2024-020.quote: match that graph with the equation that is not linear
g8-2024-020.why: The item asks which of four equations represents a linear function, with x^2 and x^3 distractors. This activity is the only required place in grade 8 where a nonlinear equation is separated from linear ones: A = pi r^2 is matched to the curved graph while d = 60t and q = 50 - 0.4d go to the lines. The losing reading, 8.5.8 Linear Functions, is second best because Lesson 8 defines linear functions through proportional relationships and contexts and never puts a quadratic or cubic equation in front of students to reject; the only other nonlinear equation work, Lesson 18's 'A Square Base', sits in an optional lesson.

g8-2024-033.quote: If yes, is it a linear function? Explain your thinking.
g8-2024-033.why: The item gives a table (2.5 with 7.5, 3.5 with 10.5, 4.5 with 13.5, 5.5 with 16.5) and the key is 'linear because the rate of change is constant' -- so the item asks for the reason, not just the classification. This warm-up is where students take numeric pairs (12 inches at 0 hours, 10 at 1, 5.5 at 3) and decide whether the relationship is a linear function by testing whether the change is constant. The losing reading, 8.5.8 Linear Functions, is second best because Lesson 8 states the connection between constant rate and linearity in its synthesis but no Lesson 8 activity hands students tabulated values and asks whether they are linear.

g8-2024-035.quote: What is the volume of this cylinder? Express your answer in terms of
g8-2024-035.why: The item gives a large can (radius 3.5, height 10) and a small can (diameter 7, height 6) and asks for the difference of their volumes in terms of pi. Every step it needs is this activity: the first problem is a cylinder of height 4 and diameter 10, where students convert diameter to radius, find the base area and give the volume in terms of pi, and the silo problem repeats it from a diameter. The losing reading, 8.5.14 Finding Cylinder Dimensions, is second best because Lesson 14 runs the computation backwards -- it gives the volume and asks for a missing radius or height -- which is not what the item asks; the item supplies every dimension. The subtraction itself is asked nowhere in the unit; Lesson 15's cool-down comes nearest, asking for the volume of each of two figures but not their difference.

g8-2024-045.quote: Find the slope of the line that passes through each pair of points.
g8-2024-045.why: The item gives two ordered pairs of a linear function and asks for the rate of change, with no context and no graph. This cool-down is that task three times over, on bare pairs of points, and it is where the curriculum tests the skill. The losing reading, 8.5.9 Linear Models, is second best because Lesson 9 does work from two observations (a candle at two times, the moon on two days), but every one of its activities asks whether a linear model fits a situation rather than asking for a rate; searching all of Unit 5, no required activity asks for a rate of change from two bare points -- Lesson 8's 'Which Is Growing Faster?' is the nearest and it is optional. The unit boundary is real here: the arithmetic this item wants is taught and assessed in Unit 3.

g8-2025-039.activity: Toward a More General Slope Formula
g8-2025-039.quote: Describe a procedure for finding the slope between any two points on a line.
g8-2025-039.why: The item gives a five-row table for a linear function (-18/-6, -8/-1, 0/3, 4/5, 6/6) and asks for the rate of change, which is 1/2 from any two rows. This activity is where students build exactly that procedure -- take the vertical change over the horizontal change between any two points -- and the lesson's cool-down 'Different Slopes' (page 137) then tests it on bare pairs. The losing reading, 8.5.9 Linear Models, is second best for the same reason as g8-2024-045: Unit 5 never asks for a rate of change from tabulated values. Medium rather than high because the curriculum poses this from points and graphs rather than from a table; the one activity that names a rate of change from a table, 8.3.4's 'Comparing Two Different Representations', handles only proportional tables, and this table has a non-zero intercept, so dividing y by x would give the wrong answer.

g8-2025-041.activity: Is It Filling Up or Draining Out?
g8-2025-041.quote: Which tank started out with more water?
g8-2025-041.why: David's charges arrive as a table (17.50 at half an hour, 20.00 at 1, 25.00 at 2) and Lisa's as y = 6x + 12, and the item asks for the difference between the two one-time maintenance fees -- a comparison of initial values across two representations. That is this activity's first question, asked of a tank given by an equation against a tank given by a description. The losing reading, 8.5.7 Connecting Representations of Functions, is second best because Lesson 7 never asks for an initial value. Medium confidence, and worth a teacher's attention: at p = 0.23 this is the hardest item in the set because the table has to be extrapolated back to x = 0, a step Unit 5 never asks for -- its nearest instance is 8.3.5's Stacking Cups, where the intercept is the hidden height of the first cup below the rim.

g8-2025-043.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
g8-2025-043.quote: match that graph with the equation that is not linear
g8-2025-043.why: The item asks students to classify y = 3x + 8 and y = x^2 + 2 as linear or nonlinear. As with the two multiple-choice versions, this activity is the only required place where an equation is picked out as not linear -- A = pi r^2 against d = 60t and q = 50 - 0.4d -- and the curved graph is the reason given. The losing reading, 8.5.8 Linear Functions, is second best because Lesson 8 builds the idea of a linear function from proportional contexts and tanks but never puts a squared equation up for rejection.

g8-2026-011.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
g8-2026-011.quote: a graph in which each input does not give exactly one output
g8-2026-011.why: The item shows four graphed relations and asks which is not a function; the answer is the sideways V, where one input has two outputs. The second problem of this activity is the curriculum's own example of exactly that: Priya's distance from the starting line as she runs out and back produces a graph where each input does not give exactly one output. The losing reading, 8.5.2 Introduction to Functions, is second best because Lesson 2 is where the definition of a function is built, but it works entirely from questions and input-output diagrams -- it never puts a graph in front of students, and the item is purely graphical.

g8-2026-014.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
g8-2026-014.quote: match that graph with the equation that is not linear
g8-2026-014.why: The item asks which of y = 2x, y = 2x^3, y = x^2 - 2 and y = x^2 - x is a linear function. Same evidence as g8-2024-020 and g8-2025-043: this activity is the only required place in grade 8 where a nonlinear equation is separated from linear ones. The losing reading, 8.5.8 Linear Functions, is second best because it establishes what a linear function is but never asks students to reject a quadratic or cubic equation; Lesson 18's 'A Square Base' does contrast a nonlinear volume function with earlier linear ones, but Lesson 18 is an optional lesson.

g8-2026-019.activity: Is It Filling Up or Draining Out?
g8-2026-019.quote: connect features of an equation representing a function to what that means in a context
g8-2026-019.why: Given y = 3x + 30 for a hot-chocolate fundraiser, the item asks what the 3 and the 30 mean -- profit per cup and a one-time donation. That is this activity's stated purpose, worked on A = 200 + 8t: the 200 is what the tank started with, the 8 is the per-minute rate, and students must say which is which and how they can tell. The losing reading, 8.5.9 Linear Models, is second best because Lesson 9's subject is whether a situation can be modelled by a line at all; none of its activities asks what the two parameters of an equation mean in context.

g8-2026-026.quote: Determine the vertical intercept and explain what it represents in this situation.
g8-2026-026.why: The item shows a line on a coordinate plane and asks for the rate of change and the y-intercept together, with distractors turning on the sign of the slope. This cool-down asks for that same pair off a graph -- calculate the slope, then determine the vertical intercept -- and Lesson 6 is where the vertical intercept is introduced and interpreted. The losing reading, 8.5.9 Linear Models, is second best because reading a slope and an intercept off a given line is never asked in a required Unit 5 activity: Lesson 8's warm-up 'Bigger and Smaller' reasons only about the signs of an unlabelled graph's slope and intercept, and Lesson 8's 'Which Is Growing Faster?', which does read both off a graph, is optional. Medium: the item is decontextualized and has a negative slope, while this cool-down is a savings graph with a positive one -- the negative case is 8.3.9 and 8.3.10's contribution.

g8-2026-027.activity: Is It Filling Up or Draining Out?
g8-2026-027.quote: The amount of water starts at 400 gallons and is decreasing at 5 gallons
g8-2026-027.why: Company A is described in prose ($180.00 set-up plus $49.00 per hour) and Company B by the equation c = 99h + 150, and the item asks how the per-hour charges compare. This activity has exactly that structure -- one function as an equation, the other as a description with a starting amount and a per-minute rate -- and asks students to compare the rates and the starting values. The losing reading, 8.5.7 Connecting Representations of Functions, is second best because it compares functions in different representations but only on particular input-output values, never on rate of change, which is the only thing this item asks about.

g8-2026-037.quote: students work with data to determine if the situation represented by the data
g8-2026-037.why: The item shows four tables and asks which represents y as a linear function of x; only D (2 with 6, 4 with 10, 6 with 14, 8 with 18) has a constant rate of change, the others being squaring, cubing and 2x^2. This warm-up is where the curriculum hands students numeric pairs and asks them to decide, by checking whether the change is constant, whether the relationship is a linear function. The losing reading, 8.5.8 Linear Functions, is second best because no Lesson 8 activity presents tabulated values for a linearity judgement. Medium, with a caveat worth knowing: the three nonlinear patterns here are never met as tables in the course -- Unit 5 meets nonlinearity only as volume functions, in Lessons 17 and the optional 18.

g8-2026-044.quote: When did she turn off the water faucet?
g8-2026-044.why: The item gives a distance-time graph in five labelled segments and asks which show Sean resting -- that is, which segments are flat. This activity hands students a piecewise graph of the water in a tub and asks them to read the events off its segments: when the faucet was turned off (where the rise becomes flat), how much water was in the tub while the dog was bathed (the flat part), how long the tub took to drain. The same lesson's cool-down 'Lin's Phone Charge' and its practice problem about a bike trail ('During what times did the rider stop?') repeat the item almost word for word. The losing reading, 8.5.6 Even More Graphs of Functions, is second best because its 'Sketching a Story about a Boy and a Bike' does tie 'stayed there for a while' to a flat piece, but it runs story to graph, whereas the item and Lesson 10 run graph to story.
